quote: Wie drücken sich ferner diese Maxima-Mini= mabedingungen durch Herumlaufen in den complexen Mannigfaltigkeiten, aus?
english: Further, how are these maxima-minima conditions expressed through going around in the complex manifolds?
topic: The page ends a question about expressing algebraic functions of several variables and maxima-minima conditions through congruences with respect to module systems, then states and begins proving a theorem that a continuous function uniformly approximated by rational functions which approximately satisfy a rational differential relation is differentiable and satisfies the differential equation F = 0.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert asks how the conditions for maxima and minima (critical points) of an algebraic function of several variables, which he had just expressed algebraically as congruences modulo module systems (ideals generated by the partial derivatives), can be described topologically. He wants to describe them through loops (monodromy, 'Herumlaufen') in the associated complex manifolds or varieties. In modern terms: describe the critical points of a polynomial or algebraic function f: C^n -> C, and in particular real maxima and minima, through the topology of the complex level sets f = c, the monodromy around the critical values, and the vanishing cycles. This is the subject of Picard–Lefschetz theory, together with Morse theory.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's question is too loosely stated to have one definitive answer. The closest established theory is Picard–Lefschetz theory: É. Picard (with Simart) did it for complex surfaces in 1897, S. Lefschetz extended it to higher dimensions in 1924 ('L'analysis situs et la géométrie algébrique'), and M. Morse's critical point theory followed in the 1920s–30s. Later work on real morsifications and monodromy (A'Campo, Gusein-Zade, 1970s) links real critical points directly to the complex monodromy. None of these sources mentions Hilbert's note, so the connection is our own interpretation.

evidence.claim: Picard–Lefschetz theory studies the topology of complex manifolds by looking at the critical points of a holomorphic function on them. Picard introduced it for complex surfaces (Picard & Simart 1897), and Lefschetz extended it to higher dimensions in 1924.
Each critical point has a vanishing cycle. The monodromy around each critical value is a (Dehn) twist along that vanishing cycle (the Picard–Lefschetz theorem).
Current research still asks how the monodromy of vanishing cycles behaves for real polynomials with real critical points, e.g. f(x,y)=g(x)+h(y).
Morse theory and Lefschetz pencils are standard tools that relate critical points to the topology of complex varieties.

triage.why: The note is a short side question and gives no precise formulation, so it can only be matched to later work by interpretation. Read as asking how the critical points (maxima and minima) of algebraic functions show up in monodromy around complex manifolds, it lines up with Picard–Lefschetz theory: Picard 1897, Lefschetz 1924, and later Morse theory, real morsification and vanishing-cycle theory. These fields developed partly after Hilbert's note and are still actively researched. The question is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. No source found connects this specific note to any later work, so 'solved' means only that the area it points to was developed by others.
